name: Jotform
whyPeoplePay: Jotform sells a form builder that someone who has never written a line of code can drive on a Tuesday afternoon, plus the boring parts nobody wants to own: the hosting, the uploads bucket, the payment connectors, the e-signature flow and the template library you start from instead of a blank page. The bill is metered on the two things you cannot control, how many forms you keep and how many people answer them, so a form that does well is the one that moves you up a tier.

plans.name: Starter
plans.note: Free forever: 5 forms, 100 submissions a month, 10,000 monthly form views, 100 MB of upload space, 10 payment submissions and 10 signed documents a month, 100 fields per form.

plans.name: Bronze
plans.note: 25 forms, 1,000 submissions a month, 100,000 monthly views, 1 GB of uploads, 100 payment submissions and 100 signed documents a month. $34/mo billed annually, which the page shows as $408 a year.

plans.name: Silver
plans.note: 50 forms, 2,500 submissions a month, 1,000,000 monthly views, 10 GB of uploads, 250 payment submissions and 250 signed documents a month. $39/mo billed annually, shown as $468 a year.

plans.name: Gold
plans.note: 100 forms, 10,000 submissions a month, 10,000,000 monthly views, 100 GB of uploads, 1,000 payment submissions and 1,000 signed documents a month, and HIPAA features. $99/mo billed annually, shown as $1,188 a year.

plans.name: Enterprise
plans.note: Quote only. This is the row where the caps read unlimited and where more than one person gets an account.

pricing.note: The pricing page builds its plan table in JavaScript, so we read it once and corroborated the monthly and annual figures against an independent search: 39/49/129 a month, or 34/39/99 a month billed annually, with the annual totals of $408, $468 and $1,188 reconciling exactly. The submission, form, view and upload caps are recorded as the table gave them. The row we are least sure of is the one labelled total submission storage, whose 500 / 10,000 / 25,000 / 100,000 figures the page prints without a unit, so we have left it out of the plan notes rather than guess what it counts.

ranked.rationale: The closest match to the shape Jotform actually sells: a drag-and-drop builder with the ordinary field types, conditional logic, file uploads, themes and a submissions inbox, on a hostname you own and with no monthly submission meter deciding your bill. Three containers and an evening, which is the cheapest entry on this page. What you give up is the parts Jotform bolts on around the form: payment connectors, e-signature workflows, HIPAA paperwork and the template library.

Pick this instead when the goal is surveys rather than forms: one question at a time, an in-product widget that catches people while they are still using your app, and drop-off and completion analytics as a first-class feature. It answers the Typeform question more precisely than the Jotform one, and it costs a seven-service stack and a weekend to run, so it is second here on install cost rather than on quality.

The research-grade option, and the only one on this list built for questionnaires that have to survive a methodologist: quotas, randomisation, panel tokens, offline collection, question types nobody else ships. It comes from a different design era than Jotform and looks it, so choose it when the logic in the questionnaire matters more than the impression the form makes.

evaluatedNotTested.name: OpnForm
evaluatedNotTested.note: Actively developed, and the nearest visual rival to HeyForm for the classic multi-field form: Laravel and Vue, a hosted plan alongside the source. Its licence file is AGPLv3 with a carve-out for an api/app/Enterprise directory under a separate licence, which is why GitHub reports it as unclassified rather than AGPL. We have not tested it, and that carve-out is the thing to read before you build on it.

evaluatedNotTested.name: Form.io
evaluatedNotTested.note: Actively developed, OSL-3.0, and a different product than the others here: a form and data-management platform meant to be embedded in an application you are already building, with a JSON schema, a REST API and a renderer you drop into your own front end. Self-hosting it is a development project rather than an install, so it is the right answer only if a developer is going to own it.

evaluatedNotTested.name: OhMyForm
evaluatedNotTested.note: Archived. The repository has been read-only since 2024 and takes no issues or pull requests, so nothing gets a security fix. It still turns up near the top of every search for an open-source Typeform or Jotform replacement, which is the only reason it is listed: so you know it is finished before you spend an evening on it.
